"He's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America," he said. Trump's speech in eastern Michigan on Sunday came a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's elections. At Saturday's rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks by El-Sayed's opponents as an attempt to make him look "less patriotic and less American than they are." The former president compared them to his experience as the target of [USN:KBN23O2P2 TEXT:"false claims"] that he was born in Kenya. "We have seen this movie before," Obama said. "I starred in it ... This stuff didn't work on me. Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul." MANUFACTURING INVESTMENTS Port Huron is part of an area of Michigan that Trump won in the 2024 presidential election with more than 66% of the vote. One issue in focus during the campaign in the state has been the US-Canada tariff standoff, which has affected the Detroit-based [USN:L6N44N11O TEXT:"US auto industry"] and prompted Rogers to distance himself from the president's policy. Rogers on Sunday hailed Trump's tariffs for securing manufacturing investments for Michigan by Chevrolet and Detroit Diesel, but said "the automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit." "There's some good and there's some things we have to work on," he told "Meet the Press." In a Fox News interview ahead of Sunday's rally, Trump praised Rogers as someone who shares Michigan voters' beliefs. "He's going to be an amazing senator," Trump told the "Sunday Briefing" program. "Solid as a rock. Apple pie." Democrats need to gain just a handful of seats each in the US Senate and House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

item.title: Brazil's Lula takes early lead in presidential runoff vote
item.description: Corruption scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of US meddling dominated the race.
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Brito, Luciana Novaes Magalhaes, Brendan O'Boyle
item.content:encoded: President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva took an early lead in Brazil's presidential runoff on Sunday evening, as results began reporting after a Supreme Court-mandated pause injected confusion into an already tight and tense runoff race. With just over 5% of tallies reported, Lula was leading right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro, with around 51.16% versus Bolsonaro's 48.84%. A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a bulwark against Washington's influence in the region as his government has pushed back on US trade and security policies. Yet the contest threatens to be overshadowed by legal disputes after Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, who was formerly Lula's lawyer, accepted a request by Lula's campaign to extend voting, pointing to public transportation issues in three cities in the state of Bahia. Zanin's decision landed right around the election's 5 p.m. Brasilia time (2000 GMT) cutoff, creating confusion as some polling stations had already closed. In a subsequent ruling, Zanin said those stations would remain shut, allowing authorities to begin tallying those votes, but that polling stations that had not closed after the official cutoff could keep receiving voters for an additional two hours. Zanin's ruling led the electoral court, or TSE, to pause the count for two hours. PAUSE ADDS UNCERTAINTY The unexpected voting extension injects uncertainty into a Brazilian electoral process still grappling with the fallout from 2022, when Jair Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat to Lula. His supporters later invaded government buildings in protest against the result, and Bolsonaro received a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup. Two legal experts told Reuters the extension of voting hours and allegations around disrupted public transportation could draw legal challenges. “Depending on the election result, there is a possibility that the losing side might attempt to contest the outcome, arguing that many people were unable to vote even with the extended deadline," said Vera Chemim, a constitutional lawyer in São Paulo. The senator's brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, speaking on a live stream on his YouTube channel, questioned why the Supreme Court had ruled in a process overseen by the country's federal electoral court: "Strange, isn’t it?" he said. "It’s hard to imagine what the legal basis for this could possibly be. It doesn’t inspire credibility.” Lula had asked electoral authorities to extend voting in at least nine states after his campaign alleged some officials reduced election-day public transportation, impacting voters' ability to get to the polls. Earlier on Sunday, a court in Bahia, a Lula stronghold in the Northeast, ordered the arrest of a top transportation official in the city of Salvador over allegations that he directed a reduction in the city’s bus fleet. In comments before Zanin's decision, Lula said "something abominable is happening" in this election. Flavio Bolsonaro had also asked for voting to be extended in at least three states, citing bad weather. WASHINGTON IS WATCHING Lula and his allies see Sunday’s runoff as a chance to stem Latin America's conservative drift. Reuters on Saturday [USN:L1N4650X8 TEXT:"revealed a campaign"] within Trump's State Department to help get the Bolsonaros back in power. Trump has so far declined to endorse a candidate. Asked on Sunday who he hoped would win, Trump declined to say. "I don’t want to get into that, but we are watching," he told reporters in Washington.

item.title: Aleksandar Vucic concède la défaite aux élections législatives en Serbie
item.description: Le dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic a concédé la défaite aux élections législatives, alors que les Serbes se sont massivement rendu aux urnes dimanche pour chasser du pouvoir un président que nombre d'entre eux, à commencer par les étudiants qui ont multiplié les manifestations depuis deux ans, accusent de corruption.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic a concédé la défaite aux élections législatives, alors que les Serbes se sont massivement rendu aux urnes dimanche pour chasser du pouvoir un président que nombre d'entre eux, à commencer par les étudiants qui ont multiplié les manifestations depuis deux ans, accusent de corruption. "Nous n'avons pas encore les résultats définitifs mais (...) il est clair que nous avons perdu les élections. Le Mouvement des étudiants aura entre 135 et 140 sièges et nous en aurons 105", a-t-il déclaré. Aleksandar Vucic a démissionné de ses fonctions de président le mois dernier après avoir annoncé la tenue d'élections anticipées, dans une tentative visant à prolonger son emprise sur le pouvoir en se présentant à nouveau au poste de Premier ministre. De longues files se sont formées devant les bureaux de vote dans tout le pays, et même Aleksandar Vucic a dû patienter deux heures avant de déposer son bulletin dans l'urne. A 18h00, le taux de participation s'élevait à 67,6%, le plus élevé depuis l'éclatement de la Yougoslavie en 1992. Aleksandar Vucic a été confronté à des manifestations anti-corruption déclenchées par l'effondrement, en novembre 2024, du toit de la gare de la ville de Novi Sad, dans le nord du pays, qui a tué 16 personnes. La victoire de l'opposition estudiantine constitue un profond bouleversement politique dans ce pays des Balkans comptant quelque 6 millions d'habitants. Elle pourrait également servir de modèle à d'autres mouvements étudiants à travers l'Europe, qui sont descendus dans la rue ces dernières semaines pour protester, parfois violemment, contre la mauvaise qualité de l'enseignement et le manque de perspectives d'avenir. Depuis son accession au pouvoir en 2014, Aleksandar Vucic a supervisé une période de développement économique mais a également dû faire face à un mécontentement croissant face à ce que ses opposants qualifient de corruption et d'autoritarisme.

item.title: Serbia's Vucic concedes defeat in historic election win for student protest movement
item.description: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country.
item.dc:creator: Ivana Sekularac, Edward Mcallister, Aleksandar Vasovic
item.content:encoded: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power and heralds a new political era in the Balkan country. Vucic, a populist and nationalist, has dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president since 2014. But he called snap elections in September after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. "It is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won," Vucic said in a televised speech. Within moments of his announcement, the streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration before the crowd swelled into the tens of thousands, with cars honking, people dancing and students shouting "victory" and "he's done". The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban in April. It may also offer a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently , against poor education standards and a lack of prospects. Vucic said the students would have between 135 and 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament and that his SNS party will have 105, based on preliminary results. "Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. "Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future." RECORD TURNOUT SPURS STUDENTS TO VICTORY Lines of unprecedented length had snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across the country earlier in the day, and even Vucic waited for nearly two hours to vote in Belgrade. Pollsters and the election commission put turnout close to 70%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992. "(The turnout) did not surprise me because there was a large and strong mass that has formed throughout the past two years," said voter Katarina Petrovic. Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, was a strong incumbent and few in the student protest movement dared believe that he would concede so fast. Supporters credit him with modernising Serbia's economy and building new highways, railways, schools and hospitals. "Some businessmen, some people will leave us but our structure is firm, we are very united, very strong, we are used to being in the opposition," Vucic said. UNCERTAINTY OVER THE STUDENTS' CANDIDATES Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare. Their list of 250 largely unknown personalities includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is still unclear who will be prime minister. The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vucic allies in the police, security services and ministries. But the students have been quieter on their international ambitions. As Vucic did for years, they will have to juggle relations with China, a major investor, Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, and the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner. PROTEST MOVEMENT INCREASED PRESSURE The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster started small but quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups and activists say repression has worsened in the period since. "For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," said actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, at a Belgrade polling station. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. He said the students are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss. Meanwhile, on the streets of Belgrade, a traditional brass band struck up, and a group including a man in a "students are champions" jumper floated balloons in the shape of the number 3, representing the number of the students' list of candidates. "We will drink a beer to celebrate, we will get drunk, we are so happy, I have no words to describe how much," said Andjela, a student who was with a group of friends.

item.title: Sydney's new international airport opens to passengers
item.description: Sydney's new A$5.6 billion ($3.94 billion) airport opened to passengers on Sunday after more than a decade of planning, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said was a milestone for the country's most populous city.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Sydney's new A$5.6 billion ($3.94 billion) airport opened to passengers on Sunday after more than a decade of planning, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said was a milestone for the country's most populous city. The new Western Sydney International Airport in Badgerys Creek, about 60 km (37.3 miles) west of central Sydney, will operate 24 hours a day, giving [USN:L1N42I00H TEXT:"airlines"] access to a fast-growing and ethnically diverse population centre. The current airport, located closer to Sydney's central business district, can host takeoffs and landings only until 11 p.m. and after 6 a.m., limiting airline scheduling options relative to other major Australian cities like Melbourne. "For the first time in more than 50 years, Australia is opening a major new airport. It’s a milestone that has been decades in the making," Albanese said in a statement. "I’m very proud to officially open it," he said. Qantas' (QAN.AX) budget arm Jetstar was due to operate the first outbound flight to the Gold Coast on Sunday, the airport said in a statement. The airport has capacity for more than 80 million passenger movements annually, it said. The start of passenger services comes after cargo flights commenced at the facility in July. Located on a 1,780-hectare (4,398-acre) site purchased by the federal government in the 1980s, the airport was completed in July 2025 after a seven-year build and 15 years of planning. ($1 = 1.4219 Australian dollars)

item.title: Saudis say Riyadh airport partly reopens despite renewed Houthi threats
item.description: Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday even as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a "military target".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia said its main airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday even as Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis vowed to keep striking the facility, which they called a "military target". King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had halted operations on October 10 following an attack claimed by the Houthis that killed 13 people, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia said it intercepted another wave of missiles and drones on Sunday as fighting with the militant group continued unabated. The Houthis said they had launched attacks on the air hub among other sites in the kingdom, including in Khamis Mushait and Jazan. It was not immediately clear if those were the strikes the kingdom said it had blocked. The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising element in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran , turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war. FLIGHT TRACKING DATA SHOWS LITTLE TRAFFIC After Saudi authorities announced the partial resumption of operations at the airport, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree vowed the facility would "never be safe" and urged airlines, airport staff and travellers not to use it. Late on Saturday, the airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday. Despite the announcement, flight tracking data from Flightradar24 showed little traffic at the airport on Sunday. The Saudi-led coalition said earlier this month that the Houthis had carried out 20 attacks on the airport between October 1 and 11. MISSILE AND DRONE ATTACKS CONTINUE Saudi civil defense said on Sunday that shrapnel from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis over Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah injured two people and damaged residential buildings and vehicles. Civil defense authorities earlier issued emergency alerts for Riyadh and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran on Sunday, before saying minutes later that the danger had passed. The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait. It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements. Saudi Arabia has stepped up its strikes against the Houthis after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, closing in on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a global maritime chokepoint and shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz. The renewed fighting in Yemen has shattered a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government, after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa a year earlier.

item.title: Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
item.description: Two US State Department officials pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Stargardter
item.content:encoded: Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter. Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration. The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who [USN:L1N3ZM12Y TEXT:"oversees Brazil policy"], and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported. Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said. In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said. After Bolsonaro received a [USN:S0N3UJ08N TEXT:"27-year sentence in September 2025"], the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said. Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department. State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections." Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests. Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration. Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed." SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of " free speech diplomacy ," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies. The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions. Moraes did not respond to a comment request. Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America. Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court. Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power. Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption. Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so. Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment. Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said. The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts. A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy." TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime. Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups. In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time. Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those [USN:S0N3ON011 TEXT:"announced against Mexican cartels"] in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said. Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees. The State Department announced the designation the following day. Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision. BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil. Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said. Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS (JBSS.O) - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down. Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March [USN:S0N3ZG01R TEXT:"Brazil barred Beattie"] from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity. Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory. "Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

item.title: OFRMO Summary
item.description: La prix Nobel Maria Corina Machado est rentrée au Venezuela
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La prix Nobel Maria Corina Machado est rentrée au Venezuela CARACAS, 25 octobre (Reuters) - La cheffe de file de l'opposition vénézuélienne, Maria Corina Machado, a annoncé dimanche être rentrée dans son pays après avoir passé près d'un an dans la clandestinité à l'étranger. Elections législatives en Serbie, l'opposition tente de renverser Vucic BELGRADE, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Serbes se rendent aux urnes dimanche alors que les opposants du dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic, qui a accédé au pouvoir en 2014, l'accusent de corruption. Les Brésiliens aux urnes pour un second tour serré entre Lula et Bolsonaro SAO PAULO/RIO DE JANEIRO, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Brésiliens ont commencé à voter dimanche pour un second tour de la présidentielle qui s'annonce serré et qui pourrait faire basculer le plus grand pays d'Amérique latine vers la droite, comme nombre de pays de la région. Ouchakov, conseiller de Poutine, prône une implication européenne dans les efforts de paix en Ukraine MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Europe doit être impliquée dans les discussions sur une issue au conflit entre l'Ukraine et la Russie car sa position pourrait être déterminante, a déclaré dimanche Iouri Ouchakov, conseiller diplomatique du président russe Vladimir Poutine. L'Arabie saoudite intercepte des missiles et des drones 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Arabie saoudite a intercepté dimanche des drones et des missiles au-dessus de sa capitale Ryad et du sud de son territoire, a dit la coalition emmenée par les Saoudiens contre les Houthis au Yémen. Russie-Trois morts dans des attaques dans la région de Belgorod MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Deux personnes ont été tuées et 13 autres blessées dans la nuit de samedi à dimanche par une attaque de drone ukrainienne contre la ville de Belgorod, en Russie, près de la frontière entre les deux pays, ont déclaré les autorités locales.
